o1.biggest_strength: A tight, calm series built on the two habits that predict retention. Email 3 branches by signup platform, Email 4 is a guilt-free inactivity check-in, and the drop list is backed by our own numbers.
o1.biggest_mistake: The last slot goes to a Pro pitch instead of finishing the habit work. It also leans on a feature claim (time reminders are Pro) that I'd need to check, and users who never add a task never get the recurring-task email.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Use email 5 to push whichever habit the user is missing. Add a day-based fallback so users who never add a task still get email 2. Include an at-a-glance table of sends and skips.

o2.biggest_strength: The whole series serves the two habits. Email 5 sends only the missing step. There are fallback send days for every trigger, a clear at-a-glance table with skip rules, and measures sized to our volume (1,800 people a quarter per point).
o2.biggest_mistake: The control group gets no onboarding emails at all, not even the welcome. That is a costly holdout. Pro also disappears from the series without a plan for revenue in the first month.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Hold back a control group that keeps the old series, or a bare welcome only. Give a concrete post-day-30 Pro plan with its own measure. Trim a little to stay safely under 1,200 words.

reason: Both are usable and on-voice, but the second spends every email on the two habits that matter, with smarter fallbacks and a 'missing step' finale. The first gives the last slot to a Pro pitch.
